1) Answer to your prompt

I can’t prove that Senator Bernie Sanders “disregards human rights.” On the contrary, the verifiable record shows frequent efforts to advance human rights, alongside a few decisions and statements that critics argue fell short.

Examples commonly cited as advancing human rights:
- Led the successful 2019 War Powers effort to end U.S. support for the Saudi‑led war in Yemen, a conflict widely described as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis at the time. The Senate passed the resolution on March 13, 2019; Sanders’ office and independent reporting document his leadership role. ([sanders.senate.gov](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/sanders-statement-on-passage-of-yemen-war-powers-resolution-2/?utm_source=openai))
- Forced floor votes in 2024–2025 to condition or halt U.S. arms transfers to Israel over civilian harm and aid blockages in Gaza (his measures failed, but they explicitly rested on U.S. human‑rights and arms‑export laws). Votes occurred January 16, 2024, November 2024, and April 3, 2025. ([sanders.senate.gov](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/fact-sheet-502bc-of-the-foreign-assistance-act-and-senator-bernie-sanders-resolution-on-israel-and-gaza/?utm_source=openai))
- Consistently high civil‑liberties and rights ratings from major watchdogs (e.g., ACLU scorecard for the 117th Congress: 100%). ([aclu.org](https://www.aclu.org/scorecard/legislators/vt-bernard-sanders/?utm_source=openai))

Criticisms sometimes raised—and what the record shows:
- 2005 gun‑industry immunity (PLCAA): As a House member, Sanders voted “Yea” on S.397 (Oct 20, 2005), which curtailed certain civil liability suits against firearms makers; in 2016 he said he would co‑sponsor repeal. Supporters say the law prevents abusive suits; critics say it reduces accountability for victims. ([clerk.house.gov](https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/2005534))
- 2007 comprehensive immigration bill: Sanders voted “Nay” on cloture for the Kennedy substitute to move the bill forward (June 7, 2007). He argued at the time—and later—that the guest‑worker provisions were abusive; fact‑checks note that his explanation is partly accurate but omits some context. Critics say the “Nay” delayed reforms benefiting millions. ([senate.gov](https://www.senate.gov/legislative/LIS/roll_call_votes/vote1101/vote_110_1_00206.htm))
- Remarks on Cuba/Nicaragua/USSR: Sanders has been criticized for highlighting social programs while, in critics’ view, minimizing repression (e.g., 2020 “60 Minutes” Cuba‑literacy comments and older 1980s remarks). He has also repeatedly condemned those regimes’ authoritarianism. Reasonable people disagree on the weight of these statements; they do not demonstrate a pattern of “disregarding human rights.” ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/feb/24/bernie-sanders/sanders-correct-cuba-literacy-campaign-skimps-prop/?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: The available, sourced evidence does not substantiate the categorical claim that Sanders “disregards human rights.” It shows a generally pro‑human‑rights record with a few contested votes and statements that are debated in context. ([sanders.senate.gov](https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/sanders-statement-on-passage-of-yemen-war-powers-resolution-2/?utm_source=openai))
